title: TikTok Video Script Examples: What a Working Script Actually Looks Like
markdown:
# TikTok Video Script Examples: What a Working Script Actually Looks Like

You can film. You can edit. You own a ring light and a tripod and three transitions you're proud of. Then you open a blank document to write the actual words for the video, and nothing comes.

This is a specific, common failure point, and it's rarely named. Most creator advice covers hooks and trends and posting times. Almost none of it covers the fifteen minutes before any of that, when a creator stares at a cursor trying to turn "I have a video idea" into a script with a beginning, middle, and end.

The fix isn't a better outline template. Templates don't know your topic. What actually closes the gap is something that can take a one-line idea and return a structured, timed script: hooks ranked by strength, a beat-by-beat voiceover and on-screen text breakdown, and a caption ready to paste. That's the job a Capafy skill called tiktok-script-pro was built to do.

## What actually stalls creators

Three things, consistently:

The hook. Most people know the first three seconds matter, but knowing that doesn't tell you which sentence to open with. A flat opener kills watch time before the video has a chance to prove itself.

The structure. A script needs to move from hook to build to payoff to a call to action, and each beat needs a matching visual cue, not just words. Writing voiceover without planning the shot that goes under it produces a mismatch you only notice in the edit, when it's expensive to fix.

The caption. Hashtags and a posting tip feel like an afterthought, but a caption with no hashtag strategy or no filming note is a missed chance to extend reach for free.

None of these are solved by "just write faster." They're solved by having a second pass that already knows the shape a working script takes.

## What the tool returns

Here's a real example, unedited, from a request that just said: "A 30-second TikTok about why cold email still works in 2026."

**You send:** "A 30-second TikTok about why cold email still works in 2026."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Angle:** the single sharpest claim the video makes about cold email in 2026.
- **Hooks (3, one marked RECOMMENDED):**
  1. *Contrarian* — "Everyone says cold email is dead. It isn't." (RECOMMENDED, with the reason it works)
  2. *Question* — "Why did this cold email get a 40% reply rate?"
  3. *Stat-style* — a hook built only from facts you supplied.
- **Timed script table:** voiceover · on-screen text · visual/shot cue, beat by beat, HOOK → BUILD → PAYOFF → CTA.
- **Caption:** 4–6 hashtags plus one filming or posting tip.

Notice what's missing: no vague advice, no "consider adding a hook here." Every output is a line you can read on camera or paste straight into the app. The ranked hooks matter because a flat list of three options with no recommendation just moves the decision problem one step down the line. This version makes the call and tells you why.

The timed table is the part that saves the most time in practice, because it forces the voiceover and the visual to exist in the same place at the same time, instead of being figured out separately and reconciled in the edit.

## When this is worth using

If you already have a system that works, a video skeleton you reuse, and a hook formula that's converting, you probably don't need this. The tool is built for the moment before that system exists: the first draft of a script, a format you haven't tried before, or a topic you know cold but can't find the angle for.

It's also useful as a second opinion. If you have a script you like but want to pressure-test the hook against two alternatives, running the same idea through and comparing is a fast way to check whether your instinct was actually the strongest option.
